transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-07 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Alice Ramos (Redwood AE), Ben Cho (Redwood SE), Lena Park (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (Stargrove Infra), Tom Ellis (Stargrove Head of Cloud), Ravi Patel (Stargrove Security), Joan Marquez (Stargrove DevOps)

Summary:
Quick discovery to understand Stargrove's private onramp needs for Redwood Private: VPC peering vs privatelink, region gating (EU+APAC), egress IPs, KMS/HSM integration, and timeline for pilot.

Topics:
- Current infra and constraints
- Network topology (transit gateway, peering, private endpoints)
- Security controls (KMS, audit logs, SSO)
- Latency and failover requirements
- Next steps and PoC scope

Action items (briefed above)

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alice Ramos: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alice, I'm the AE for this account. we'll keep this short, just want to map requirements for a private onramp. Ben and Lena from our SE team are here to dig into the network stuff.
[00:18] Maya Singh: Hey, thanks, I'm Maya - infra. We've got about 15 minutes to go over the high level then we'll bring in the internal network folks if needed.
[00:27] Tom Ellis: Tom here. main things for us: data residency for eu, some apac clusters later, and we need static egress IPs or a known egress set so our firewalls can be updated.
[00:39] Ben Cho: Great, that's exactly what we usually start with. can I ask what your current cloud provider footprint looks like? single account or multi-account?
[00:48] Joan Marquez: multi-account on AWS, we've got central transit in a hub account using TGW, then app VPCs in each region.
[00:56] Ben Cho: ok, TGW is fine. do you have any policy that prevents VPC peering across accounts?
[01:05] Maya Singh: We generally avoid cross-account peering for management reasons, prefer privatelink and TGW. peering is allowed but our security team flags it as harder to manage.
[01:13] Ravi Patel: yeah, peering is OK technically but change control is heavier. we prefer endpoints we can manage via central account.
[01:20] Alice Ramos: Understood. so Redwood Private can be deployed in a couple of shapes: a VPC in your account with private endpoints to our control plane, or we can host a customer-dedicated VPC and peer it - both have tradeoffs. Ben, do you want to run the topology?
[01:33] Ben Cho: Sure. Option A: PrivateLink-style endpoints — you create an interface endpoint in your VPC that talks to a private endpoint we provision in our controlled environment. That avoids peering and fits TGW routing. Option B: direct VPC peering across accounts for lower per-request latency and simpler routing, but requires you to accept peering and manage CIDR overlap. Option C: host Redwood nodes in your VPC as a customer-managed private deployment (on-prem style) - more work but full data plane control.
[02:02] Tom Ellis: latency is a moderate concern. our inference traffic is bursty; we want to keep tail latency under 120ms 95th for small prompts in region. Does the PrivateLink add meaningful latency?
[02:14] Ben Cho: In our benchmarks PrivateLink adds typically 10-25ms depending on region, peering can shave that so peering is lowest latency. But PrivateLink is operationally simpler for teams that won't accept peering.
[02:25] Joan Marquez: Another constraint: our CIDRs overlap with some vendor ranges. we use 10.0.0.0/8 internally in many accounts - so peering could be messy.
[02:33] Maya Singh: yeah overlap is the killer. We can carve out a /22 for external connectivity if needed but we'd need approvals.
[02:41] Lena Park: If you can carve a /22 for the onramp that usually makes peering a lot simpler. otherwise PrivateLink is the fallback.
[02:50] Ravi Patel: On the security front, we need KMS integration, so keys are customer-managed for any data-at-rest, and an audit log for every request. SOC2 is a must. can redwood support a customer KMS or HSM?
[03:03] Ben Cho: We support customer-managed keys via KMS integration for sensitive artifacts. For Private we can support envelope encryption where you control the master key, and we store material encrypted. HSM is a little more bespoke, but we've done HSM integrations for customers — need to scope.
[03:16] Tom Ellis: And the logs — we prefer forwarding audit logs to our SIEM. Is there a log-forwarding option?
[03:23] Alice Ramos: Yes, we have audit log streaming (S3 or syslog) and you can forward to your SIEM. we'll include the runbook showing fields and retention.
[03:32] Maya Singh: What about region constraints? we can't have data egress to us-east for EU workloads. We need the inference to stay in eu-west-1 for EU customers.
[03:42] Ben Cho: Absolutely. Redwood Private can be deployed per-region. for EU-only workloads we can pin model endpoints to eu-west-1 nodes and not route across regions. We also support a region-gating policy at routing layer.
[03:55] Joan Marquez: Do you have a list of supported regions and matrix of latency/cost per region?
[04:01] Ben Cho: We'll share a region matrix. quick note — APAC presence is still expanding; for APAC we usually recommend a nearby dedicated cluster or using a partner colo.
[04:12] Tom Ellis: Ok. One more — our security team requires SAML SSO with SCIM and RBAC integration for auditability. support?
[04:20] Alice Ramos: Yes SSO via SAML/OIDC + SCIM provisioning, role-based access controls in the console, and token-level audit trails. we'll attach the SSO integration guide.
[04:30] Ravi Patel: Thanks. network ops will want to see exact port lists and egress IP ranges. can you provide static egress IPs or a publishable set?
[04:39] Ben Cho: For private deployments we can publish a set of egress IPs per deployment. for hosted we have dynamic pools so not guaranteed; for dedicated/private we can reserve elastic IPs and give them to you.
[04:51] Maya Singh: And TLS termination - do you handle certs or does customer manage?
[04:57] Lena Park: We support both. by default Redwood terminates TLS in our control plane, but if you want certs behind your load balancer in your VPC we can accommodate mutual TLS or customer certs on the endpoint.
[05:11] Tom Ellis: What about autoscaling? if we burst do you have a warm pool or gradual ramp? we don't want cold starts to affect latency.
[05:20] Ben Cho: For Private we support warm node pools and pre-warming policies; we also support burst capacity for unexpected peaks. for Dedicated deployments you can set reserved capacity. we'll include suggested autoscale policy configs.
[05:33] Joan Marquez: Can we do canary routing or fallback to a smaller model in case of capacity constraints?
[05:39] Ben Cho: Yes traffic routing can fallback to a smaller quantized model in same region. Redwood supports automatic fallback policies and canary rollouts for model versions.
[05:50] Maya Singh: Ok great. Now the practical ask - if we do PrivateLink into our TGW, how's DNS handled? we need internal DNS entries so our apps call a friendly name.
[06:00] Lena Park: With interface endpoints you create a DNS CNAME to the endpoint or use private hosted zones. we provide guidance; if you're using TGW, you may need conditional forwarding in your resolver. we've seen customers push a private hosted zone into the shared resolver.
[06:13] Ravi Patel: Is there any issue with cross-account DNS resolution? we prefer not to open broader resolver permissions.
[06:19] Ben Cho: You can keep DNS scoped, we typically recommend creating private hosted zones in the TGW's route for consistent resolution. that's part of the topology sketch we'll send.
[06:28] Alice Ramos: Quick devops question — do you have specific ports locked down? e.g., will we need to open 443 only or also gRPC ports?
[06:36] Joan Marquez: Our corporate policy only allows 443 outbound to vendor endpoints unless there's a strong reason.
[06:41] Ben Cho: 443 is sufficient for typical inference traffic; we can multiplex over HTTPS so no extra ports needed.
[06:47] Maya Singh: One complexity — we have dedicated on-prem racks that talk to cloud via a VPN. if we wanted a hybrid deployment (some nodes on-prem, some in cloud) is that possible?
[06:58] Ben Cho: Yes hybrid is possible. we support on-prem connectors that register with the control plane over a secure tunnel; model weights can be pinned locally and inference stays local. For heavy data locality customers this is a common pattern.
[07:12] Tom Ellis: That would help with APAC latency but increases ops. might be a phase 2.
[07:18] Alice Ramos: timeline — what are you targeting for a pilot?
[07:21] Tom Ellis: We'd like to run a pilot in oct-nov timeframe, with a small footprint in eu-west-1. execs want a cost/latency readout and SOC2 paperwork before green light.
[07:31] Alice Ramos: Sounds good. Ben we'll prepare an initial topology + cost estimate for eu-west-1, and security pack.
[07:38] Ben Cho: i'll also note we need the CIDR ranges you mentioned and whether TGW can host the endpoint.
[07:45] Maya Singh: We'll action CIDR confirmation post-call. Also: do you support token-level billing + per-route visibility? we want to see token costs per model for the pilot.
[07:56] Alice Ramos: Yes we provide token-level cost breakdowns in the console and per-route dashboards; we can export CSVs for finance.
[08:04] Joan Marquez: Any known constraints on NAT gateway throughput? our NATs can be a bottleneck during heavy bursts.
[08:12] Ben Cho: If you route through NATs you need to ensure they scale. we often avoid NAT bottlenecks by placing endpoints in the TGW peering path or assigning static egress IPs from a dedicated NAT. we'll detail best practices.
[08:25] Ravi Patel: Ok. A compliance detail: can Redwood attest to data deletion — if we request logs/artifacts removed, is that supported?
[08:33] Lena Park: We support retention policies and also support on-demand deletion for customer data. Deletion is auditable and we'll include the retention API.
[08:43] Tom Ellis: Are there any SLA numbers for Private? uptime/latency SLAs?
[08:48] Alice Ramos: For Private deployments we offer SLA-backed SLAs on availability and latency tiers on Dedicated contracts. For pilot we'll propose a standard uptime pledge and discuss higher SLAs for enterprise term.
[08:59] Maya Singh: A small nit - we need to know whether the control plane ever sees plaintext data or if it's all encrypted client-side prior to sending.
[09:08] Ben Cho: By default payloads are encrypted in transit. if you need end-to-end encryption we can discuss client-side encryption options, but that can limit some control-plane features like evals. we'll include a write-up.
[09:20] Joan Marquez: Great. Anything else?
[09:23] Tom Ellis: Can you confirm the people we should involve next call? networking (TGW owner), security (Ravi), platform (Joan), and bench infra guy.
[09:32] Alice Ramos: Perfect, we'll invite networking and schedule a deeper technical session.
[09:36] Ben Cho: We'll also prepare a simple connectivity checklist: CIDRs, TGW capability, who will own endpoints, SIEM forward details, KMS requirements.
[09:46] Maya Singh: One more question — do you support IP allowlisting per API token? we'd like tokens tied to a source IP.
[09:54] Lena Park: Yes, for private deployments you can restrict tokens by source IP and also by route. we'll document recommended pattern.
[10:03] Alice Ramos: Ok wrapping up. Quick recap: Redwood will send security pack + SOC2 and SSO docs, an initial VPC topology sketch with PrivateLink and peering options, and a region latency/cost matrix. Stargrove will confirm CIDR ranges and whether TGW can host endpoints, and security will send KMS/HSM questions. We'll reconvene for a technical deep-dive.
[10:27] Tom Ellis: sounds good, thanks everyone.
[10:31] Maya Singh: thanks.
[10:34] Ravi Patel: thanks all.

Notes:
- Shared artifacts referenced during call: "Redwood Private runbook" (link sent post-call), "region latency matrix" (will be attached), initial topology sketch (ASAP).
- Minor transcription artifacts: speaker labels sometimes merged; some proper nouns (e.g., TGW vs "T G W") transcribed inconsistently.
